He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach who has worked with players including Trevoh Chalobah. They spend four days on the pitch and days in between in the gym. A typical day begins at 9am with an hour of activation and stretching before Dele heads to non-league Windsor & Eton at 11am, where he trains on the pitches and uses the facilities. Culture.title: Roll up, roll up! Marc Chagall’s Circus is the most mesmerising big top you’ve ever seen – review
Culture.summary: Hepworth Wakefield, West Yorkshire He spent over 60 years painting clowns, ringmasters and acrobats – and the results transport you to a dazzling magical world At the opening of The Circus, a self-portrait of Marc Chagall is placed next to a lithograph of a clown. The portrait is small and sketched simply in a blue crayon, as if Chagall had quickly dashed it out to pacify an inquisitive fan. In contrast, the clown is rich in colour and texture, with a heavily detailed backdrop of musicians, spectators and performers. But there is something uncanny about this pairing, created more than 40 years apart. They both wear small, brimmed hats with hair springing out from underneath, and their facial expressions are somewhat inscrutable. It is the perfect introduction to an exhibition that explores Chagall’s lifelong fascination with the circus, both as a subject and as a symbolic motif. In placing Chagall and the clown side by side, we understand this immediately – the clown is both a clown and a metaphor for the artist. In his 1967 art book Cirque, Chagall writes: “This clown – he is he and I.” Continue reading...

Culture.title: ‘It’s peak Aussie – and it’s fantastic!’ How Australian TV conquered the world
Culture.summary: From Colin from Accounts to a certain blue heeler dog, Australian TV has swept the globe – so much so that many kids have picked up the accent. Homegrown stars and creators explain how down under went overground About four years ago, parents around the world began observing a strange phenomena in their children: Australian accents. Bluey – the charming cartoon about a dog and her family that is currently one of the most watched shows in the world – had children saying words such as “dunny” and “brekky” without thinking twice. “When I was a kid, I would do an American accent when I played with my toys,” says Daley Pearson, co-founder of Ludo Studio, which makes Bluey. “So this is like the colony taking back over!” Continue reading...
